Blood Administration

Level: Advanced
Topic: Critical Care / Trauma
Duration: 75 minutes

Arrival Scenario

You’re transporting a 42-year-old male from a rural ED to a trauma center. GSW to abdomen, emergent ex-lap, lost 2 liters in the OR. He’s hypotensive (BP 82/50), tachy (HR 135), pale, and cold.

The surgeon hands you 4 units of PRBCs and 2 units of FFP. “He needs these on the way. Massive transfusion protocol. You good?”

You better be.

Because when you’re moving blood, mistakes kill fast.

Warm-Up Questions

Before we get into protocols, answer these:

  1. What’s the maximum hang time for a unit of blood?
  2. Can you run blood through the same line as normal saline?
  3. **What happens if you give

ABO-incompatible blood?**

  1. What’s the difference between PRBCs, FFP, and platelets?
  2. What are the signs of a transfusion reaction?

Think through it. These aren’t theoretical—they’re life-or-death.

Explanation / Breakdown

Blood Product Basics

Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs)

  • What it is: RBCs with most plasma removed
  • What it does: Carries oxygen, increases Hgb
  • Volume: ~300 mL per unit
  • Raises Hgb by: ~1 g/dL per unit
  • When to use: Hemorrhage, severe anemia (Hgb < 7), symptomatic anemia

Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)

  • What it is: Liquid portion of blood with clotting factors
  • What it does: Replaces clotting factors, corrects coagulopathy
  • Volume: ~250 mL per unit
  • When to use: Massive transfusion, warfarin reversal, coagulopathy, DIC

Platelets

  • What it is: Concentrated platelets from multiple donors
  • What it does: Stops bleeding, helps clotting
  • Volume: ~300 mL per unit
  • When to use: Thrombocytopenia (< 50K in bleeding patient), platelet dysfunction

Cryoprecipitate (“Cryo”)

  • What it is: Concentrated fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF
  • What it does: Provides fibrinogen for clot formation
  • When to use: Hypofibrinogenemia, massive transfusion, DIC

Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP)

In massive hemorrhage, you don’t transfuse one product at a time. You give balanced resuscitation:

1:1:1 Ratio

  • 1 unit PRBCs : 1 unit FFP : 1 unit Platelets (per 6-pack)

Why? Giving only PRBCs dilutes clotting factors and causes coagulopathy. Balanced resuscitation prevents this.

Activation criteria:

  • Loss of 1 blood volume in 24 hours
  • 50% blood volume in 3 hours

  • 4 units PRBCs in 1 hour

  • Shock + ongoing bleeding

Blood Compatibility

ABO Compatibility Chart

Recipient Can Receive Universal?
O- O- only Universal Donor
O+ O-, O+ —
A- O-, A- —
A+ O-, O+, A-, A+ —
B- O-, B- —
B+ O-, O+, B-, B+ —
AB- O-, A-, B-, AB- —
AB+ All types Universal Recipient

In emergencies:

  • Use O- PRBCs (universal donor)
  • Use AB plasma (universal donor for plasma)

Type-specific is better than O- when available. O- is precious—save it for true unknowns.

Administration Rules

1. Verify blood product TWICE

  • Check patient name, DOB, blood type
  • Check unit number, expiration, integrity
  • Two providers confirm (you + nurse/medic)

2. Use proper tubing

  • Blood administration set with 170-micron filter
  • NEVER use a standard IV set

3. Compatible fluids

  • Normal saline ONLY
  • No LR (calcium binds citrate in blood)
  • No D5W (causes hemolysis)

4. Warming

  • Use a blood warmer for rapid transfusion
  • Prevents hypothermia-induced coagulopathy
  • NEVER microwave or use hot water

5. Hang time

  • Maximum 4 hours per unit
  • After 4 hours, blood must be discarded
  • Start a new unit if not infused

6. Rate

  • Trauma/hemorrhage: wide open (pressure bag, rapid infuser)
  • Stable patient: 2-4 hours per unit
  • Watch for volume overload in cardiac/renal patients

Transfusion Reactions

Acute Hemolytic Reaction (ABO incompatibility)

Timing: Immediate (within minutes)
Signs: Fever, chills, back/chest pain, hypotension, dark urine, shock
Action: STOP transfusion immediately, maintain IV with NS, treat shock, notify blood bank

Febrile Non-Hemolytic Reaction

Timing: Within hours
Signs: Fever (> 1°C rise), chills, mild discomfort
Action: Slow/stop transfusion, give acetaminophen, monitor closely

Allergic Reaction

Timing: Minutes to hours
Signs: Urticaria (hives), itching, flushing, mild respiratory symptoms
Action: Stop transfusion, give Benadryl (diphenhydramine), may resume if mild

Anaphylaxis

Timing: Immediate
Signs: Severe respiratory distress, angioedema, hypotension, shock
Action: Stop transfusion, epi 0.3-0.5 mg IM, aggressive airway management, IV fluids

TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury)

Timing: Within 6 hours
Signs: Acute respiratory distress, hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates, no fluid overload
Action: Stop transfusion, supportive care (O2, CPAP, intubation if needed)

TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload)

Timing: During or shortly after
Signs: Dyspnea, hypertension, JVD, crackles, pulmonary edema
Action: Stop/slow transfusion, sit patient upright, diuretics, O2, CPAP

Common Mistakes

Mistake #1: Using the Wrong IV Line

Blood + D5W = hemolysis. Blood + calcium-containing fluids = clotting. Use NS only.

Mistake #2: Skipping the Double-Check

Giving incompatible blood is catastrophic. Always verify twice with two people.

Mistake #3: Running Blood Too Slow in Hemorrhage

In massive bleeding, RUN IT WIDE OPEN. Use a pressure bag. Seconds matter.

Mistake #4: Ignoring Early Transfusion Reactions

Fever, chills, back pain in the first 15 minutes? STOP THE BLOOD. Don’t wait.

Mistake #5: Forgetting to Warm

Cold blood causes hypothermia → coagulopathy → more bleeding. Always use a warmer.

Mistake #6: Over-Transfusing Stable Patients

Not everyone needs a Hgb of 10. Restrictive strategy (Hgb 7-8) is often better.

Clinical Pearls

💎 O- PRBCs are liquid gold. Use type-specific when possible. Save O- for unknowns.

💎 1:1:1 saves lives. In massive transfusion, balanced resuscitation prevents coagulopathy.

💎 Check within 15 minutes. Most acute reactions happen early. Stay at bedside.

💎 Hypothermia kills. Warm the blood, warm the patient. The lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy) is real.

💎 Back pain during transfusion = hemolytic reaction until proven otherwise. Stop immediately.

💎 Platelets don’t work if patient is cold. Warm first, then transfuse.

💎 AB plasma is universal donor plasma. In emergency MTP, use AB plasma if type-specific unavailable.

💎 Document everything. Unit numbers, times, vitals, reactions. Medicolegal and quality control.

💎 When in doubt, STOP. You can always restart. You can’t undo a fatal reaction.

Decision Trees

Blood Administration Checklist

Pre-Transfusion
    ↓
1. Verify order/indication
2. Obtain consent (if possible)
3. Check patient ID band
4. Two-person verification of blood product
5. Check expiration date
6. Inspect product (no clots, discoloration, leaks)
7. Baseline vitals
8. Establish IV access (18G or larger preferred)
9. Prime blood tubing with NS
10. Set up blood warmer (if available)
    ↓
Start Transfusion
    ↓
During Transfusion
    ↓
1. Vitals at 15 minutes, then q30 minutes
2. Monitor for reactions continuously
3. Adjust rate based on clinical status
4. Document unit number, start time
    ↓
Post-Transfusion
    ↓
1. Final vitals
2. Document completion time
3. Monitor for delayed reactions
4. Dispose of tubing/empty unit per protocol

Transfusion Reaction Response

Reaction Suspected
    ↓
STOP TRANSFUSION IMMEDIATELY
    ↓
Maintain IV access with NS (new line if possible)
    ↓
Check vitals
    ↓
Assess type of reaction:

Fever + back pain + hypotension?
    → HEMOLYTIC REACTION
    → Aggressive fluid resuscitation
    → Treat shock
    → Send blood sample + urine sample
    → Notify blood bank STAT

Respiratory distress + hypoxia?
    → TRALI or TACO?
    → TRALI: bilateral infiltrates, no JVD → Supportive care, O2
    → TACO: hypertension, JVD, crackles → Diuretics, CPAP

Hives + itching?
    → ALLERGIC REACTION
    → Benadryl 25-50 mg IV/IM
    → Monitor airway
    → Mild? May resume transfusion slowly

Severe respiratory distress + angioedema?
    → ANAPHYLAXIS
    → Epi 0.3-0.5 mg IM
    → Airway management
    → Aggressive treatment

Fever only, no other symptoms?
    → FEBRILE NON-HEMOLYTIC
    → Acetaminophen
    → Monitor closely
    → May resume if mild

Practice Cases

Case 1: The Trauma Patient

Patient: 28-year-old male, MVC, ruptured spleen, in OR for 2 hours
Status: BP 78/40, HR 142, cold/clammy, 6 units PRBCs given so far
Lab: Hgb 5.2, INR 2.1, platelets 45K

What blood products do you anticipate needing?

Click for answer **Answer:** Continued balanced MTP: PRBCs, FFP, Platelets (1:1:1 ratio) **Why:** - Ongoing hemorrhage with shock - Coagulopathy developing (INR elevated, platelets dropping) - Needs balanced resuscitation to prevent "dilutional coagulopathy" **Action:** - Activate MTP if not already done - Prepare 4 more units PRBCs, 4 FFP, 1 platelet pack - Consider TXA if < 3 hours from injury - Keep patient warm (blood warmer, Bair Hugger) - Massive transfuser if available

Case 2: The Reaction

Patient: 65-year-old female, GI bleed, receiving 2nd unit of PRBCs
Event: 20 minutes into transfusion, patient reports severe back pain, fever 101.8°F, BP dropping to 88/52

What’s happening and what do you do?

Click for answer **Answer:** Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction **Why:** - Back pain + fever + hypotension during transfusion = classic triad - Suggests ABO incompatibility (wrong blood type given) **Action:** - STOP transfusion IMMEDIATELY - Disconnect blood tubing (do NOT flush line) - Start new IV with NS, run wide open - Treat hypotension (fluids, pressors if needed) - Save the blood unit and tubing (send back to blood bank) - Draw blood sample (hemolysis labs: bili, haptoglobin, LDH) - Catch urine sample (check for hemoglobinuria) - Notify blood bank and physician STAT - Prepare for DIC, renal failure

Case 3: The CHF Patient

Patient: 80-year-old female, CHF (EF 25%), symptomatic anemia
Lab: Hgb 6.8
Orders: Transfuse 2 units PRBCs

What’s your concern?

Click for answer **Answer:** Risk of TACO (volume overload) **Why:** - CHF patients have poor cardiac reserve - Each unit = 300 mL of volume - High risk of pulmonary edema **Action:** - Transfuse slowly (2-4 hours per unit minimum) - Pre-medicate with diuretic (Lasix 20-40 mg IV) if ordered - Monitor closely: vitals q15 min, lung sounds - Watch for: increased work of breathing, crackles, hypoxia, hypertension - Keep head of bed elevated - Stop immediately if signs of overload

Case 4: The Unstable Type

Patient: 34-year-old male, stab wound to chest, hypotensive, type unknown
Surgeon: “He needs blood NOW. We don’t have time to type him.”

What do you give?

Click for answer **Answer:** O- PRBCs and AB plasma (universal donors) **Why:** - O- blood has no A or B antigens (won't react with any antibodies) - AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies (won't attack patient cells) - This is the safest emergency combination **Action:** - Give O- PRBCs immediately (pressure bag, wide open) - Give AB plasma (or type-specific if known soon) - Send type and cross NOW (results in 30-45 min) - Switch to type-specific as soon as available - Document "emergency release" protocol used

Case 5: The Delayed Reaction

Patient: 52-year-old male, received 2 units PRBCs yesterday for GI bleed
Now: Fever 100.9°F, mild SOB, urticaria on trunk

What is this?

Click for answer **Answer:** Delayed allergic/febrile transfusion reaction **Why:** - Occurred hours after transfusion (not immediate) - Fever + urticaria suggests immune response - Could be febrile non-hemolytic or delayed allergic reaction **Action:** - Benadryl 25-50 mg PO/IV - Acetaminophen 650 mg PO - Monitor respiratory status (TRALI can occur up to 6 hours post-transfusion) - If worsens: O2, consider steroids - Document and report to blood bank - Patient may need pre-meds (Benadryl, Tylenol) before future transfusions

Reflection

You just learned how to safely administer blood products in high-stakes situations.

Here’s what you should know cold:

✅ Blood product types and indications
✅ Massive transfusion protocol (1:1:1 ratio)
✅ ABO compatibility and universal donors
✅ Administration rules (verification, tubing, fluids, warming)
✅ Transfusion reactions (recognition and response)
✅ When to STOP and how to intervene

Next-level thinking:

  • How do you manage Jehovah’s Witness patients who refuse blood?
  • What’s the role of whole blood in trauma resuscitation?
  • How does hypothermia affect transfusion efficacy?
  • When should you consider factor concentrates vs FFP?

Your assignment:
Shadow a blood transfusion from start to finish. Observe the checks, the monitoring, the documentation. Ask questions. This is high-risk, high-reward medicine—learn it right.

Because when you’re the only thing between your patient and exsanguination, you better know what you’re doing.
